records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Plant Toolbox, Ficus benghalensis page. Under the 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading: Poison Severity: Low (human-scoped; the page's Problem for Cats / Problem for Dogs entries are separate tags and carry no severity rating). Poison Symptoms: 'If ingested by pets or humans, it can cause decreased appetite, drooling, nausea, vomiting, and diarrhea. The sap can irritate the skin.' Poison Toxic Principle: Proteolytic enzyme and psoralen. Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes. Poison Part: Leaves, Sap/Juice (full list; the page lists two parts). Problems block lists: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs, Problem for Horses, Weedy. Plant Type block lists: Epiphyte, Houseplant, Poisonous, Tree, Vine. Prose: 'Be mindful as a houseplant, the Bengal fig is toxic if ingested. Keep out of the reach of pets or children. The sap of this plant can cause skin irritation; therefore, wearing protective gloves is recommended when handling this plant.' The symptom sentence says 'pets' without naming an animal; the cat and dog scoping comes from the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags.

unknowns: Only plants.ces.ncsu.edu had a loadable dedicated page for Ficus benghalensis; RHS, MoBot, UF/IFAS, Clemson and UGA pages for this exact name could not be located or loaded (RHS and Clemson searches returned nothing usable; MoBot, EDIS and Clemson hosts refused or timed out), so no second source corroborates any field and scientific_name_accepted rests on the NC State title alone.

toxic_to_pets: NC State's symptom sentence says 'pets or humans' without naming an animal; true rests on the separate Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs tags. The page also tags Problem for Horses and Problem for Children. Poison Part lists Leaves and Sap/Juice, not Leaves alone. Poison Severity Low sits under the 'Poisonous to Humans:' heading.

is_edible set false only because the page says the plant is toxic if ingested and tags it poisonous if ingested; the page does not address the fruit as food specifically (Wildlife Value says only that the fruits attract birds) and its Ethnobotany text is medicinal use.
humidity_need high is read from 'A humidifier near your plant would help maintain high humidity' alongside the stated 50 to 80% range; no other source to confirm.

Temperature: NC State states 65 to 80 degrees Fahrenheit without separating day from night, and gives no cold-damage onset figure, so all day/night/chill fields are null. USDA zones 10a-12b is a hardiness rating, not a damage onset.

Light: houseplant prose says bright, indirect sunlight, with no foot-candle or direct-sun-hour figure, so light_fc_min, light_fc_good and direct_sun_hours_max are null. outdoor_sun_exposure comes from NC State's structured Light field (Full sun; Partial Shade) which is the in-ground tree rating.

Soil pH: houseplant prose says neutral pH and the structured field says Neutral (6.0-8.0); soil_ph_min 6.0 is the lower edge of that band; soil_ph_max left null because no second source (RHS) was available to check the closed top of the band.

Watering: no interval in days is stated, so water_growing_days_est and water_dormant_days_est are null. water_check_depth_cm 5 is the 2-inch lower end of 'top 2 to 3 inches' converted at 2.54 cm per inch (range 5.1 to 7.6 cm).
Fertilizing: the page says to use a liquid fertilizer during the growing season from spring through summer, with no interval or dilution strength, so interval, strength and months are left null.

Size: NC State has no Dimensions block for this species. The only figure is the wild-tree statement 'It can grow up to 100 feet tall', so mature_height_in_max is 1200 in and the minimum is null; that figure applies to the species grown outdoors as a tree in frost-free climates, not to a potted houseplant. No spread is stated ('wide spreading crown' only; 'more than 60 feet' is Available Space To Plant, not spread). 'Audrey' at 1 to 2 feet tall is a cultivar size and is not the species'. The page also says 'Houseplants do not produce the aerial roots that are common in the wild.'
Outdoors the species is described as a serious weed problem since introduction in Florida and can kill its host tree; the Problems list includes Weedy.

records.name_note: NC State's page title parenthetical lists Air Plant, Giant Air Plant, Xerographic Air Plant, in alphabetical order; its Common Name(s) list shows the same three entries stacked. Giant Air Plant was chosen because NC State's own description prose refers to the plant as 'the giant air plant'. The plain name 'Air Plant' was not used as the primary name.
unknowns: Only one admissible source had a dedicated page for this exact taxon: plants.ces.ncsu.edu. The RHS, Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS and Clemson pages could not be loaded or had no page for this species (RHS URLs 404 or returned another plant, plantfinder.mobot.org and edis/ask.ifas hosts were blocked, Clemson returned 403), so no cross-source confirmation was possible.

NC State's Common Name(s) list gives Air Plant, Giant Air Plant and Xerographic Air Plant; none is 'Xerographica Air Plant'. Air Plant was not used because it is the genus-wide umbrella name (the page itself refers to 'air plants' as a group) and the catalog already holds Tillandsia ionantha as Air Plant; Giant Air Plant is the name the page's description prose uses for this species.
toxic_to_pets, toxicity_detail left null: the NC State page carries no toxicity block and names no cat or dog hazard for this species.
is_edible left null: the page does not address eating the plant.
attracts_pollinators left null: the page has no Attracts field and no pollinator statement.

chill_damage_f left null: NC State says only that it is 'a tropical plant intolerant of frost' and gives USDA zones 9a-11b, which are not a damage-onset temperature. Day and night temperature fields also have no stated figures.

humidity_need and the humidity percentages left null: the page says only that home heating and air conditioning can affect humidity and the plant might need more watering, and lists 'Humidity' under Resistance To Challenges; neither is a stated humidity requirement.

water_regime, water_growing_days_est, water_dormant_days_est, water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm left null: the care is a soaking routine ('Soak the plant in water for 15 minutes every 1 or 2 weeks', monthly in winter) that does not map to the soil-moisture enum, and the interval is a word-based cadence not converted to a day count. After soaking the plant must be shaken out and dried upside-down to prevent crown rot.
fertilize_interval_days left null: the page says 'once or twice a month', a word-based cadence; fertilize_active_months also null because no months are named.
soil_base, soil_drainage and the soil pH fields left null: this is an epiphyte grown without soil and the page states no medium, drainage or pH.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only. NC State's structured Light field lists both 'Full sun (6 or more hours of direct sunlight a day)' and 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)', but the species-specific care prose says 'It requires bright light but not full sunlight.' and the page's only outdoor siting advice is 'Indoor plants can spend summer months outside in the shade of a tree or pergola.' The tag '#full sun tolerant' is a tolerance trait, not a recommendation. full_sun was dropped at landing on that contradiction; part_shade rests on the Light field's Partial Shade value and the shade-siting sentence.

direct_sun_hours_max left null: NC State's species prose gives no hour figure. The '6 or more hours' and '2-6 hours' figures are part of the generic category labels NC State renders inside every Light field value, not species-specific statements.
light_fc_min and light_fc_good left null: no foot-candle figure is stated, only 'bright light' and 'A south-facing window should be sufficient'.
The NC State Height and Width range (1-3 ft each) is taken as given; the page does not say whether the height includes the 1-3 ft flower stalk.

records.toxicity_detail: Source: NC State Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox page for Philodendron hastatum. The page's warning line (under Phonetic Spelling) says "This plant has low severity poison characteristics." Its "Poisonous to Humans" block (human-scoped) gives Poison Severity: Low; Poison Symptoms: "If ingested, it can cause mouth and stomach irritation. The sap causes skin irritation."; Poison Toxic Principle: Calcium oxalate crystals; Causes Contact Dermatitis: Yes; Poison Part (full list): Flowers, Fruits, Leaves, Roots, Sap/Juice, Seeds, Stems. The page's Problems field lists: Contact Dermatitis, Poisonous to Humans, Problem for Cats, Problem for Children, Problem for Dogs. The Plant Type field lists: Herbaceous Perennial, Houseplant, Poisonous. The page's tag line includes #poisonous if ingested, #problem for children, #problem for cats and #problem for dogs, at separate (non-contiguous) places in the line. The Low severity rating comes from the human-scoped Poison block; the Problem for Cats and Problem for Dogs entries are separate tags, and the page gives no cat- or dog-specific symptoms or severity. The page gives no separate handling warning (no gloves or keep-away sentence).
unknowns: Only NC State (plants.ces.ncsu.edu) was found with a dedicated page for Philodendron hastatum. RHS (philodendron-hastatum URL) returned 404, and no dedicated page was located on the other admissible domains. plantfinder.mobot.org was not reachable in the sandbox. Clemson HGIC returned 403 and UF/IFAS EDIS returned 404 for the URLs tried. Every populated field therefore rests on the NC State page alone.
NC State renders a single Common Name(s) entry (Silver Sword Philodendron), matching the page-title parenthetical, so there is no common-name split between sources.

toxic_to_pets=true rests on NC State's Problems entries 'Problem for Cats' and 'Problem for Dogs' (and the matching tags). The Poison block is human-scoped, and the page gives no cat/dog-specific symptoms or severity.

is_edible=false rests on NC State's '#poisonous if ingested' tag and its Poison Symptoms text. No source states the plant is not edible in so many words, and the page gives low severity (mouth and stomach irritation).

The NC State page gives the Light field as 'Partial Shade (Direct sunlight only part of the day, 2-6 hours)'. direct_sun_hours_max is left null: the '2-6 hours' figure is part of the generic category label NC State renders inside every Light field value, not a species-specific statement. The prose says to avoid direct sunlight, which can scorch the leaves, but gives no hour figure. Indoor light in foot-candles is not stated, so light_fc_min and light_fc_good are null.

The page says the room temperature should average between 65 to 85 degrees Fahrenheit, with no separate day/night split and no stated cold-damage onset. Day and night temperatures and chill_damage_f are therefore null. Zone 10a-11b is a hardiness rating, not a damage-onset temperature.
humidity_need=high comes from the prose 'prefers ... high humidity'. No percentage is given, so humidity_pct_min and humidity_pct_max are null.

Watering: the page says only 'Overwatering can cause root rot.' and describes the soil as moist, well-drained. That is a soil adjective, not a watering statement, so water_regime and all watering interval fields are null. NC State's Soil Drainage tags are 'Good Drainage' and 'Moist', which maps to moderate.

Soil pH: NC State gives 'Acid (<6.0)', an open-ended band, so soil_ph_min and soil_ph_max are null. soil_base=standard_potting is a mapping from the prose 'moist, well-drained, rich soil' and Soil Texture 'High Organic Matter'. No source names a potting mix.

Size: the mature_height_in and mature_spread_in values come from NC State's Dimensions block (Height 10 ft - 15 ft = 120-180 in; Width 1 ft - 2 ft = 12-24 in), which matches the prose 'In the home, it can reach up to 10 to 15 feet tall and 2 feet wide'. The prose gives 20 to 30 feet tall when grown outdoors. The plant is a climber needing a moss pole or trellis, so the height is partly a support-dependent figure.

No fertilizer guidance and no attracts/pollinator information is on the page, so those fields are null. The page lists Deer and Rabbits under Resistance To Challenges, which is not pollination evidence.

records.toxicity_detail: NC State's tag block reads "#houseplant #non-toxic for cats #humidity tolerant #container plant #non-toxic for dogs #perennial #dappled shade #summer flowers #green leaves #spring flowers #orange bracts #terrarium #long-lasting flowers #partial shade tolerant". The only toxicity-related tags are #non-toxic for cats and #non-toxic for dogs. The page has no Poison block, so there is no severity rating, poison-part list, symptom list or handling warning. unknowns: No dedicated Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS, Clemson, UMD, PSU or UGA page for Goeppertia crocata was found. A MoBot search returned only the G. roseopicta page, and plantfinder.mobot.org was not reachable from the sandbox. Only NC State and RHS carry species-specific evidence.

RHS's Cultivation paragraph (under glass, peat-free compost, high humidity, at least 16C, water moderately, monthly balanced liquid fertiliser) is word-for-word identical on the G. roseopicta and G. insignis RHS pages. It is genus boilerplate, so it was not used for fertilize_*, water_* or temperature fields. Fertilizer fields are null.

RHS's structured Moisture field reads 'Moist but well-drained or Well-drained'. NC State shows Good Drainage plus Moist and says the soil should be evenly moist and not soggy. Together these give soil_drainage moderate. moisture_retentive is not set, because no source states consistently wet soil as a requirement for this species, and NC State warns that overwatering can cause root rot.

water_regime keep_moist rests on NC State's watering statement 'evenly moist and not soggy'. NC State gives no dry-down depth or interval, so water_dry_down_target, water_check_depth_cm and the day estimates are null.
soil_ph is null. NC State lists Acid (<6.0) and Neutral (6.0-8.0) with no ceiling or floor from an open-ended band. RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral.

NC State's prose gives one 'room temperature' range of 65 to 80 F, not a separate day/night split. It is recorded as day_f_min/max and night_f is null. direct_sun_hours_max is null: the '2-6 hours' figure is part of the generic category label NC State renders inside every Light field value, not a species-specific statement. outdoor_sun_exposure is limited to part_shade, from NC State's Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade fields and RHS Position 'Partial shade'. records.name_note: Sources split on the lead common name. NC State's page-title parenthetical lists 'Creeping Buttons, Jade Necklace, Peperomia Rotundifolia, Round Leaf Peperomia, Trailing Jade, Yorba Linda' (an alphabetized list, with Creeping Buttons first), while its Description prose leads with 'The Round Leaf Peperomia'; RHS's page title pairs the binomial with 'jade necklace'. Round Leaf Peperomia was chosen as the name the NC State Description leads with. NC State also records the former names Peperomia lanjouwii and Piper rotundifolium.
records.toxicity_detail: NC State's Tags line for this exact page reads '#trailing #epiphytic #houseplant #hanging baskets #creeping #non-toxic for cats #non-toxic for horses #non-toxic for dogs #perennial', so it carries #non-toxic for cats, #non-toxic for dogs and #non-toxic for horses alongside the trait tags. The page has no Poison block, so there is no poison-part list, symptom list or severity rating, and no handling warning. RHS carries no toxicity statement for this species.
unknowns: No toxicity statement beyond NC State's non-toxic tags; there is no Poison block, so human-scoped toxicity is unrecorded.

humidity_need is high on NC State's 'thrives in high humidity'; the same sentence says it tolerates normal household conditions, so average household humidity is acceptable. No humidity percentages are published.

outdoor_sun_exposure is part_shade only (NC State Light field: Dappled Sunlight and Partial Shade). RHS's Position field lists Full sun and Partial shade; full_sun was left out because NC State's Description says 'Avoid cold drafts and direct sunlight.' direct_sun_hours_max is null: the '2-6 hours' figure is part of the generic category label NC State renders inside every Light field value, not a species-specific statement.

soil_base, water_regime and all watering fields are null: RHS's Cultivation paragraph (houseplant compost, water moderately in summer, sparingly in winter, monthly balanced fertiliser) appears word for word on the sibling RHS Peperomia prostrata page, so it is genus boilerplate, not species evidence. NC State's 'moist, well-drained soil' is a soil adjective and 'Yellow leaves result from overwatering' is not a watering regime.
Fertilizer interval, active months and strength are null for the same reason; 'monthly' and 'spring to summer' are word cadences and 'balanced' is not a dilution fraction.
Soil pH is null: NC State's 'Acid (<6.0)' is open-ended with no floor or ceiling, and RHS lists Acid or Alkaline or Neutral.
No source states a chill-damage onset temperature; NC State's USDA zones 10a-12b are a hardiness rating and RHS H1B is a UK rating, so chill_damage_f and day/night temperatures are null.
No light foot-candle figures are published by an admissible source.

Size: RHS gives one height figure (Max Height up to 10 cm = 3.9 in, so min is null) and Max Spread 0.1-0.5 metres; RHS's description says 'to 3cm tall', which differs from the 10 cm Max Height field. NC State has no Dimensions block (its Available Space To Plant is 12 inches-3 feet and its Quick ID Hints say 'up to 12 inches long', neither is a mature-size field).
is_edible and attracts_pollinators: no admissible source addresses eating or pollinators for this species.

Trade name 'Trailing Jade' appears in NC State's common-name list for this plant; it is not the Jade Plant (Crassula ovata) or String Of Buttons (Crassula perforata). No admissible source was checked for that contrast, so it is stated here as a caution, not a sourced claim.
No Missouri Botanical Garden, UF/IFAS, Clemson, Penn State, Maryland or UGA page for this exact species was found; only NC State and RHS cover it.
